transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Elena Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Tidal Head of Security), Liam O'Connor (Tidal Platform Eng), Rajiv Menon (Tidal CTO)

Summary: quick run-through of audit logs and admin activity capture; export and retention options; encryption/KMS details; next steps captured at end.

00:00 Elena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call... we got Maya, Liam, Rajiv from Tidal, and Samir and I from Redwood, Jordan from CS. sound good?
00:12 Maya: Yep, thanks. we had a few specific questions — kinda around what exactly you log for admin activity vs user requests, and how we can export/store long term.
00:23 Samir: Great. we'll go high level then show the export paths. quick note, transcription may have a few mislabels but i'll try to be explicit.
00:35 Rajiv: Perfect. our compliance folks need to know defaults and what we can keep for like 7 years if needed.
00:43 Samir: Understood. first, what we capture: there are two main streams — audit/admin logs and request-level telemetry. Audit logs capture admin actions: role changes, RBAC policy updates, SSO provisioning events, API key creation/revocation, model rollout events, dedicated capacity changes, config changes, and user account management.
01:05 Liam: do you capture who triggered a model rollout? like if someone flips a canary?
01:09 Samir: yes, the audit record includes actor (user id/email), timestamp, action type, target resource, old/new values where applicable, and request metadata like IP and region. sometimes the "old/new" diff can be truncated for very large blobs.
01:26 Maya: what about content — the actual prompts or generated responses, are those in the audit logs?
01:31 Samir: by default, we do not include full message content in admin audit logs. request-level telemetry can include message metadata (token counts, model version, latency). message content capture is configurable: we have an optional opt-in for storing convo content in logs for debugging/poc, but that has explicit consent switches and data residency flags. most customers keep content out of audit logs for privacy.
01:55 Elena: also note for SOC 2 folks — we provide a separation: admin audit trails and optional request logging. We can provide attestation and sample logs as part of SOC 2 kit.
02:06 Maya: ok good. can you say more about the export mechanisms? we need to get logs into our SIEM and also into a cold store.
02:13 Samir: Export options: (1) Stream to customer S3 bucket (JSON files, hourly or near-real-time via Kinesis-style streaming), (2) Syslog / TCP drain to your log collector, (3) Push to SIEMs — we have connectors or produce standard JSON that Splunk/Datadog can ingest, (4) Webhook/Kafka for high-throughput streaming, and (5) On-demand bulk export for e-discovery.
02:39 Liam: is the S3 export encrypted with our KMS? we can't have Redwood manage the keys.
02:44 Samir: Yes — for S3 export you can provide a customer-managed KMS key (CMK). The objects are encrypted with that key on write. We support key rotation and will re-encrypt on request during rekey flows. We also sign exports with an envelope to provide integrity proofs.
03:00 Rajiv: what's the retention default? and can we set different retention windows for admin logs vs request logs?
03:06 Samir: Default retention in hosted is 90 days for request telemetry and 180 days for audit/admin logs. Both are configurable for Dedicated/Private customers. You can set shorter or longer retention; for long term you should export to your S3 archive or a backup. For regulatory long-term retention, we recommend streaming to your cold storage — Redwood can auto-archive daily snapshots.
03:29 Maya: is that 180 days applied to immutable backups? can logs be tampered with? we need some immutability chain for audits.
03:36 Samir: Good question — we offer append-only audit logs with tamper-evidence in Dedicated and Private deployments. For hosted customers, we provide integrity signing and retention policies; for true legal immutability we recommend export to customer-controlled S3 with object lock enabled. We also maintain event hashes internally to detect unexpected mutations.
03:58 Liam: how granular is the audit event? e.g. do you log token-level ops or only higher-level actions?
04:03 Samir: Admin/audit is action-level. request telemetry gets token counts and timing metrics but not token-level content unless the optional content capture is enabled.
04:13 Maya: on data residency — if we need logs to stay in eu-west-1, can exports be restricted there?
04:18 Samir: Yes. We can route exports to region-specific endpoints. For hosted, you can choose region and we will write exports to your bucket in that region; for Private we run control plane in your VPC/region.
04:30 Elena: quick aside — people sometimes ask about PII in logs. we support configurable redaction rules before export: regex-based, field-based (headers/body), and pre-export transformers. we can also do deterministic hashing for pseudonymization.
04:46 Rajiv: do you capture failed login attempts and MFA events?
04:50 Samir: Yes, login success/failure, MFA events, SSO assertion details (SAML response metadata but not raw assertion content), SCIM provisioning events are all captured. For SSO we also log the IdP issuer and subject mapping.
05:05 Liam: for access to logs in the Redwood console, who can see them? RBAC?
05:09 Samir: RBAC controls apply. we have roles: Admin, SecurityAdmin, Billing, Viewer, etc. Audit log access is restricted to SecurityAdmin and Admin by default; you can customize roles. Also access to exported S3 is controlled by the customer's IAM policies.
05:24 Maya: do you integrate with our SIEM for alerts? like if a privileged key is revoked unexpectedly.
05:29 Samir: Yes. We can ship alerts to your SIEM or webhook — rule-based triggers for critical events (API key creation, key rotation failures, multiple failed logins, role escalations). You can configure thresholds and destinations.
05:44 Elena: i'll note that we can also create a monitoring route that pushes to your Datadog or Splunk instance with a minimal schema.
05:50 Liam: what is the log format? newline delimited JSON? CSV?
05:54 Samir: Primary format is NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON), with a stable schema: event_id, timestamp, actor, action_type, resource, old_value, new_value, ip, region, request_id, request_path, user_agent, and optional "payload" for request metadata. We also offer compressed daily batches (gzip) for cold archives.
06:15 Rajiv: how do you handle PII in those payload fields?
06:18 Samir: by default we try to avoid storing sensitive message content. payload is metadata only unless you opt in. We support field-level redaction pre-export.
06:26 Maya: can the customer run queries on logs from the console?
06:29 Samir: For hosted, we provide basic search and filters in the Console for the retention window. For deeper analysis we recommend exporting to your SIEM or Data Lake. Dedicated customers can enable long-term indexing and query via our observability add-on.
06:45 Liam: about retention changing — if we shorten retention, do we delete copies in exports?
06:49 Samir: Redwood can expire hosted copies per policy. We do not automatically delete customer export buckets — that is under your control. If you request deletion of hosted backups within the retention window we will follow the policy and provide proof of deletion.
07:03 Maya: one thing — our legal says we need proof of chain-of-custody for exports. do you provide delivery receipts or manifests?
07:10 Samir: Yes, export manifests and delivery receipts are available. For S3 exports we provide a manifest file with checksums and signed metadata so you can verify integrity. For syslog/drain we provide sequence numbers and ingest acknowledgements where supported.
07:27 Rajiv: do you have SOC 2 artifacts to share?
07:30 Elena: yes i'm going to attach our SOC 2 Type II report and an audit-logs technical spec after the call.
07:36 Maya: great. also curious about key rotation — if we rotate our CMK, how does Redwood handle decrypting older archives?
07:42 Samir: We rely on customer KMS for key access. If you rotate but keep older key material (via KMS key history), KMS will decrypt older objects. For re-encryption we can run a rewrap job to move archives to the new key, which we perform as a service or you can run in your account.
07:56 Liam: are logs immutable if written by Redwood? or can an admin edit a log entry?
08:01 Samir: Logs are immutable by design — we don't allow editing events. For hosted customers we have forensic controls and tamper-evidence hashes. Only deletion requests are possible and are tracked.
08:12 Rajiv: what's the throughput — if we have thousands of admin events per minute during a rollout, can export keep up?
08:19 Samir: Yes — exports are buffered and streamed. For very high throughput we recommend streaming via Kafka or direct Kinesis to your account. We have backpressure strategies and will switch to batched writes when necessary; nothing should be lost.
08:36 Maya: is there rate-limiting on export endpoints?
08:39 Samir: There are sensible limits but they are configurable for Enterprise and Dedicated. We'll size the account for your expected throughput.
08:49 Elena: quick pause — any questions on encryption at rest and in transit?
08:52 Maya: yes, TLS in transit obviously?
08:54 Samir: All network communication uses TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers. Objects in S3 are encrypted with SSE-KMS if you provide a CMK, otherwise SSE-S3 with our KMS. For on-prem/private we can support HSM-backed keys.
09:09 Liam: do you publish a KMS integration guide?
09:12 Elena: yes we'll share the doc — includes grant permissions and examples for key policy.
09:18 Rajiv: how about log search access - do we expose an API for programmatic retrieval?
09:22 Samir: Yes, we provide a logs API: you can query by time range, event type, and actor, and pull NDJSON results. For bulk export we suggest S3 + manifest.
09:33 Liam: will logs contain IP addresses and geolocation?
09:36 Samir: IP is captured and you can enable geo-lookup enrichment before export if you want. That enrichment can be disabled to meet privacy constraints.
09:47 Maya: on GDPR — if a user requests deletion and message content was captured, how do you handle audit records that reference that data?
09:54 Samir: we support targeted redaction. For audit trails referencing deleted content we can redact sensitive fields while preserving the event metadata (actor/action/timestamp). We include a redaction marker in the event so auditors can see deletion was performed.
10:13 Rajiv: are there any limitations for Private deployment around audit logs?
10:16 Samir: Private gives you full control — logs stay in your VPC, you control KMS and S3, and Redwood's control plane runs per your tenancy. You get deeper retention and immutability options.
10:27 Liam: for compliance we might want to disable content capture entirely. can that be enforced org-wide?
10:31 Samir: yes, org-level policy can disable message-content logging and only allow metadata. That can be enforced via policy and audited.
10:39 Maya: what's the default retention change process? if we increase retention do you backfill?
10:43 Samir: We can backfill hosted logs from backups up to a limit — for large backfills we recommend exporting archives and loading into your own store.
10:52 Elena: quick example: we'll set a demo where we'll stream a few admin events to an S3 bucket with your CMK and show the manifest and how to verify checksums.
10:59 Rajiv: great.
11:02 (Discussion continues with specific example flows — timestamps jump as the demo plan is outlined)
22:12 Elena: starting walk-through of schema — event_id is UUID, timestamp iso8601, actor.email, action_type enum, resource.type, resource.id, diff.old, diff.new, metadata.request_id.
22:45 Maya: will the diff show full object? sometimes that's huge.
22:48 Samir: we truncate diffs beyond a size threshold and store a blob ref for large objects; you can request the blob if you have privileges.
23:05 Liam: about search performance — if we index everything does that blow up costs?
23:10 Samir: indexing has cost; we provide tiered indexing. basic indexing for admin events is included, full content indexing is an add-on.
23:25 Rajiv: what about alerts for suspicious behavior? can we feed into your out-of-the-box playbooks?
23:29 Jordan: we have some canned alert templates: key compromise, brute force login, unexpected region access. we can map them into your SIEM and also configure runbooks with the CS team.
23:45 Maya: ok, two compliance asks: (1) chain of custody + manifests, (2) retention proof for deletions. both ok?
23:52 Elena: yes, both available; manifests will be attached and deletion proofs are part of our compliance pack.
24:05 Rajiv: can you provide sample logs anonymized?
24:08 Elena: yes will attach a sanitized sample set.
24:12 Liam: do you log service account actions separately from human users?
24:15 Samir: yes service accounts have actor.type = service, and we include associated token id and scope.
24:24 Maya: any limits on how long you can keep manifests?
24:27 Samir: manifests follow the same retention policy; we recommend keeping them in your cold store indefinitely.
24:35 (short discussion on retention windows and cost estimates)
30:03 Liam: security question: if an admin rotates a key, do you log who performed rotation and from which IP?
30:08 Samir: yes. rotation events include pre/post key metadata, actor, IP, and if rotation failed we'll log error code and stack trace for debugging (stack trace only in private/dedicated or on opt-in debug mode).
30:28 Maya: about export integrity — how do we verify an exported day's file hasn't been altered?
30:32 Samir: manifest contains checksums (SHA256) and is signed with our export signing key; you can verify with the public key we provide. If you use CMK, each object has S3 etag and KMS logs.
30:48 Rajiv: any SLA around exports?
30:51 Elena: for Dedicated we offer SLA for export delivery; for hosted we guarantee best-effort and will support investigations.
31:02 Liam: do you redact tokens and keys automatically from logs?
31:06 Samir: we run automated scrubbing for common secrets patterns. However we recommend customer-side transformers for domain-specific secrets.
31:20 Maya: is there a preview of the log schema?
31:23 Samir: yes — i'll share the schema doc in the follow-up.
31:30 (conversation continues — slightly more technical back-and-forth about implementation details and demo scheduling)
42:10 Elena: recap and next steps: i'll share SOC2 and sanitized logs; Samir will set up demo S3 export; Liam to confirm retention requirement; schedule deep dive.
42:26 Maya: thanks, appreciate the clarity.
42:30 Rajiv: fine by me.
42:33 Jordan: i'll send calendar invite for follow-up.
42:36 Elena: thanks everyone, meeting adjourned.
